basis: bees ordered under a king
note: Basil’s bee discussion presents the hive as an ordered community under a king; it supplies a Christian natural-theological analogue to the commentary’s malik of the bees, though section divisions vary by edition.

basis: A shepherd searches for his one lost sheep
note: The commentary's dālle camel escapes and remains away from its owner; Thomas preserves a lost-sheep parable in which the shepherd leaves the ninety-nine and seeks the stray.

basis: one strayed sheep valued above the ninety-nine
note: This lost-sheep version has the shepherd seek the one that strayed and value it above the ninety-nine, a distinct Christian apocryphal intensification of the individual animal’s recovery.

basis: flock-tender receives milk from the flock
note: Paul’s labor argument asks who tends a flock without drinking its milk. Alongside his ox citation, this turns the material benefit of a tended flock into an analogy for the guide’s rightful support.

basis: unmuzzled ox re-read for human workers
note: Paul invokes the rule against muzzling a grain-treading ox in an argument about the support of human workers; this Christian reading turns a working animal’s claim into a claim about labor, relevant to the commentary’s tamed, load-bearing animal.

basis: Straying sheep return to the shepherd and overseer
note: The commentary calls the camel dālle when lost from its owner; Peter says his readers were straying like sheep but have returned to the shepherd who watches them.

basis: straying sheep return to Shepherd and Overseer
note: The addressees were sheep going astray but have returned to a Shepherd and Overseer; it connects wandering from the way with restoration to a guiding, responsible figure.

basis: Elders must shepherd and oversee God's flock
note: The commentary develops a leading animal whose herd follows it; Peter assigns human leaders a shepherd's oversight of God's flock, making the guide's duty explicit.

basis: shepherd the flock of God under oversight
note: The elders are told to shepherd the flock of God and exercise oversight, a specific Christian instruction about the responsibility attached to leading another’s flock.

basis: Christ is the chief shepherd
note: The commentary uses malik for the animal at the head of the herd; Peter calls Christ the chief shepherd who appears above the delegated flock leaders.

basis: forsaking the straight way and going astray
note: The text says its opponents abandoned the straight way and went astray, retaining both sides of the commentary’s road vocabulary rather than merely a general moral failure.

basis: seal says the Lord knows those who are his
note: God’s firm foundation bears a seal declaring that the Lord knows those who are his, a textual counterpart to the commentary’s visible mark and the lost camel whose owner cannot be known.

basis: perverting the straight paths of the Lord
note: The rebuke names the straight paths of the Lord and accuses its target of making them crooked, a concrete New Testament counterpart to the commentary’s path that turns aside from the qasd.

basis: overseers shepherd God’s acquired flock
note: The elders must shepherd God’s flock, which God acquired, while serving as overseers. It distinguishes the true owner from delegated guides in a way that closely illuminates the commentary’s rab/mālik and leading-animal relation.

basis: A bit directs a horse's whole body
note: The commentary says the horse's hādī may be its neck or the foremost group; James supplies a different concrete steering image, the bit by which a human turns a horse.

basis: Aramaic Rabbi as an authority title
note: The source labels rabb as an owner-title; John retains the Semitic title Rabbi and glosses it as Teacher. The likely cognate relation supplies only a title comparison here, not evidence that John’s teacher image is a flock-owner image.

basis: The good shepherd gives his life for the sheep
note: The commentary distinguishes the known owner from the camel left without one; Jesus defines the true shepherd by risking his life for the flock that belongs to him.

basis: A hired worker abandons sheep when a wolf comes
note: The commentary ties the camel to its owner and herd; John's contrast distinguishes a genuine keeper from a hired hand who does not own the sheep and flees danger.

basis: The hired hand flees because the sheep are not his
note: The commentary's mark identifies whose camel it is; John makes ownership the reason the hired worker fails to care for the flock.

basis: owner and flock know one another
note: The reciprocal knowledge of shepherd and sheep gives a direct positive counterpart to the dālla whose rab and mālik cannot be identified.

basis: Other sheep are brought into one flock under one shepherd
note: The commentary contrasts owned herds with wild flocks outside a known owner; Jesus speaks of gathering other sheep so that they become one flock with one shepherd.

basis: The shepherd knows his sheep and they follow him
note: The commentary joins owner, animal, and following leader; Jesus says he knows his sheep and they follow his voice.

basis: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name
note: The commentary says a brand identifies whose camel it is and that the stray camel's owner is unknown; John's shepherd knows and summons each animal as his own.

basis: own sheep called by name and led out
note: The shepherd calls his own sheep by name and leads them out, joining recognized belonging with a leader who initiates the flock’s movement.

basis: The shepherd goes ahead and the sheep follow
note: The commentary's malik is the animal at the head of the herd and its hadī leads the others; Jesus describes the shepherd walking ahead and his sheep following.

basis: shepherd goes ahead and sheep follow
note: The shepherd goes in front and the sheep follow his voice, the closest New Testament rendering of the commentary’s front animal/hādī followed by the rest of the herd.

basis: Sheep do not follow a stranger
note: The commentary says the herd follows its foreleader; John adds recognition as the criterion, since sheep flee from an unfamiliar voice.

basis: Mary addresses Jesus as ῥαββουνί
note: The commentary's dictionary form rabb (رَبّ) is glossed 'owner'; John's Greek preserves the Aramaic rbb title 'my teacher,' a related Semitic master-title used for a teacher rather than a livestock owner.

basis: Peter is charged to shepherd Jesus' sheep
note: The commentary's herd follows a foreleader; the risen Jesus delegates care of his own sheep to Peter, distinguishing the flock's owner from its appointed shepherd.

basis: owner unties ox or donkey and leads it to water
note: Jesus describes each person untying an ox or donkey from the stall and leading it to water, joining a known owner, a restrained domestic animal, purposeful leading, and animal provision.

basis: A shepherd searches for one sheep that strayed
note: The commentary defines a dālle camel as escaped and ownerless; Jesus' parable gives the lost animal an owner who searches until he finds it.

basis: one lost sheep sought by its owner
note: The man who loses one of a hundred sheep goes after the lost one, a direct recovery scene for the commentary’s animal separated from its owner and herd.

basis: found sheep carried on shoulders
note: After finding the lost sheep, the shepherd lays it on his shoulders with joy; this supplies the bodily return of the escaped animal that the preceding search scene alone does not state.

basis: The found sheep is brought back and celebrated
note: The commentary leaves the lost camel separated from its owner; Luke's shepherd returns with the found sheep and gathers friends to celebrate, supplying a recovery scene.

basis: Heaven rejoices over a sinner who repents
note: The commentary compares human misguidance with a camel that is lost from its owner; Luke interprets the recovered sheep as the sinner who turns back, connecting return to repentance.

basis: Jesus applies the struck-shepherd saying to his disciples' flight
note: The commentary says followers depend on their herd's foreleader; Mark quotes Zechariah's struck shepherd and interprets the scattered sheep as the disciples who will fall away at Jesus' arrest.

basis: A shepherdless crowd receives teaching
note: The commentary makes a leading animal the image behind the request to be guided; Jesus sees the crowd as sheep without a shepherd and begins teaching them, acting as guide.

basis: take my yoke and learn from me
note: Jesus’ invitation to take his yoke and learn makes animal harness a figure for guided discipleship, offering a Christian transformation of the commentary’s subdued, neck-directed animal.

basis: a sheep fallen into a pit is lifted out
note: Jesus assumes that an owner will take hold of and lift out a sheep fallen into a pit even on the Sabbath, a concrete recovery scene for the commentary’s animal left in an exposed place.

basis: A shepherd seeks a wandering sheep
note: The commentary's lost camel has no known owner; Matthew's parable has a shepherd leave the ninety-nine to seek the one that wandered.

basis: The shepherd rejoices when the sheep is found
note: The commentary describes the camel only while lost; Matthew emphasizes the owner's joy at recovery.

basis: The Father wills that none of the little ones perish
note: The commentary contrasts a lost animal with humans more lost than cattle; Matthew uses the shepherd image to say the Father seeks the vulnerable rather than letting one perish.

basis: The king separates people as a shepherd separates sheep and goats
note: The commentary places the herd-leader image beside Malik, owner of Judgment Day; Jesus' judgment scene joins royal authority with a shepherd sorting livestock.

basis: Sheep stand at the king's right and goats at his left
note: The commentary presents a herd under a leader and names the owner of Judgment Day; Matthew makes the judgment division visible by assigning the sheep and goats opposite sides.

basis: The broad road leads to destruction
note: The commentary develops the straight path alongside deviation; Jesus contrasts a broad road that many enter with the path of life, giving the wrong way a destination.

basis: Few find the narrow way that leads to life
note: The commentary's request for guidance asks for a leader and a straight route; Jesus describes the difficult path to life that few find.

basis: People are harassed like sheep without a shepherd
note: The commentary says the request for guidance needs a leader ahead of the flock; Jesus sees the crowds as sheep without a shepherd, making the human need for guidance explicit.

basis: sheep without a shepherd
note: Jesus sees the crowds as sheep without a shepherd; the image makes the lack of a leading, responsible figure the cause of a dispersed and distressed flock.

basis: The beast's mark identifies its adherents
note: The commentary's camel brand indicates whose herd an animal belongs to; Revelation's imposed mark signals allegiance to the beast, a hostile counterpart rather than the same kind of ownership.

basis: name written on the forehead
note: The Lamb’s followers visibly bear his and his Father’s name on their foreheads, a personal and covenantal analogue to the commentary’s visible brand that makes an animal’s belonging recognizable.

basis: Followers go wherever the Lamb goes
note: The commentary says a herd follows the lead animal and makes this the force of asking for guidance; Revelation describes people following the Lamb wherever he goes.

basis: followers go wherever the Lamb goes
note: The redeemed follow the Lamb wherever he goes, an explicit following relation that gives the commentary’s herd behind its leading animal a Christian eschatological form.

basis: The Lamb shepherds people to springs of water
note: The commentary combines a leading animal with pasture and the request for guidance; Revelation's Lamb becomes shepherd and guides people to springs.

basis: Lamb shepherds and guides to springs
note: The Lamb becomes the flock’s shepherd and guides them to springs of water; this striking reversal makes an animal the leader while retaining the commentary’s guide-and-pasture movement.

basis: God's servants receive a seal on their foreheads
note: The commentary's brand identifies the camel's owner; Revelation's seal marks those who belong to God and are protected, transferring ownership-identification to people.

basis: identifying signs for restitution
note: The discussion of simanim in the law of lost property makes an identifying sign the means by which an item can be restored; it is a direct legal analogue to the camel’s wasm/sīmah by which it is recognized.

basis: Lost property is returned by identifying signs
note: The commentary says a camel's brand reveals its owner, while a stray camel has an unknown owner; the Bavli's reading of Deuteronomy's return law uses identifying signs to establish who may reclaim a found object.

basis: Moses follows a runaway lamb to water
note: The midrash has Moses pursue a lamb that has run from Jethro’s flock, find it drinking, and carry it back; God makes that care the reason he can shepherd Israel, joining the stray animal, water/pasture, and qualified leader.

basis: when a roadside animal counts as lost
note: The mishnah distinguishes an animal merely grazing on a road from one whose state shows genuine loss, then requires return; it gives a legal test for the commentary’s concrete dālla rather than equating every free animal with a lost one.

basis: A faithful ruler shepherds the Lord's flock in pasture
note: The commentary's malik is the herd's foreleader and its hadī guides followers; this Jewish royal hope joins a shepherd-ruler to faithful care and a pasture where sheep do not stumble.

basis: The shepherd-king leads the flock in holiness
note: The commentary joins the foreleading malik to the guide who takes a herd along a path; this Jewish royal psalm continues its shepherd image by saying the king will lead the people in holiness.

basis: God turns people back like a shepherd his flock
note: The commentary's camel is lost from its owner; Sirach compares God's correction and teaching to a shepherd bringing back his flock.

basis: Lord’s mercy trains and turns back like a shepherd
note: Sirach describes the Lord’s compassion as rebuking, training, teaching, and turning creatures back as a shepherd turns his flock; it gathers the commentary’s merciful rab, tamed animal, straying, and restoration into one Jewish formulation.

basis: The king goes out before the people
note: The commentary cites the dictionary form milk (مَلِك) for the animal at the head of a herd; Hebrew melek is its Semitic cognate, and Israel asks for a king who will go before them in battle.

basis: Hebrew melek is a ruler who goes before the people
note: The commentary's dictionary form milk (مَلِك) names the animal at the head of a herd; Hebrew melek is a cognate ruler-title, and this verse gives the king the specific role of going before Israel.

basis: Hebrew melek goes before the people
note: Hebrew melek is cognate with the commentary’s m-l-k label, and this verse asks for a king who will go before Israel; its own context thus pairs the cognate title with the front-leading function the commentary gives to milk.

basis: Israel is scattered like sheep without a master
note: The commentary connects losing a camel's owner with the need for a leader; Micaiah sees Israel dispersed on the hills like sheep without a shepherd, then sent home because they have no master.

basis: Straying ox or sheep must be returned
note: The commentary's dālle camel has escaped its owner; Torah treats a neighbor's stray livestock as recoverable property and forbids ignoring it.

basis: straying ox or sheep
note: The command to return a brother’s ox or sheep that has gone astray gives the commentary’s escaped animal a concrete action and owner relation rather than treating “straying” as an abstraction.

basis: Keep the animal until its absent owner seeks it
note: The commentary defines the stray camel as remaining where its owner is unknown; this law makes the finder temporarily responsible when the owner is not nearby.

basis: unknown owner; restore the animal
note: The verse anticipates finding a straying animal when its owner is not near or is not known, keeping it until the owner seeks it, and restoring it; this is a close legal counterpart to the dālla camel whose rab/mālik is unknown.

basis: working ox must not be muzzled
note: The law preserves the feeding claim of an ox while it works, adding an ethical limit to treating the commentary’s tamed, useful animal solely as a bearer of human benefit.

basis: Blessing includes cattle and flock offspring
note: The commentary explains its source form en-naʿam as livestock that brings good and blessing; Deuteronomy lists the increase of cattle and flock among God's covenant blessings.

basis: God goes before to lead by the way
note: The Lord goes before Israel in the pillar to lead them on the way, giving the request for guidance a concrete leading-before movement like the commentary’s hādī.

basis: Return an enemy's straying ox or donkey
note: The commentary's ownerless camel prompts the question of the finder's relation to its owner; Exodus extends recovery duty even to an enemy's animal.

basis: enemy’s wandering ox or donkey
note: Even an enemy’s wandering ox or donkey must be returned; the scene joins a loose pack animal to the obligation created by its known owner.

basis: donkey lying under its burden
note: The command to help an enemy’s donkey collapsed under its load gives an ethical counterpart to the commentary’s carrying mount: its legs bear burdens, so the human associated with it must assist.

basis: God himself searches for his sheep
note: The commentary's lost camel has an unknown owner; Ezekiel answers with God personally seeking and rescuing his scattered flock.

basis: A shepherd gathers a scattered flock
note: The commentary's animal is lost in a desolate place; this verse compares God's search to a shepherd inspecting his flock and rescuing sheep dispersed on a cloudy day.

basis: God settles his sheep in good pasture
note: The commentary develops merabb as the place camels stay and a pasture the land's inhabitant likes; Ezekiel's shepherd puts the recovered flock on good grazing land.

basis: good pasture and secure lying down
note: God promises good pasture where the flock will lie down, a precise counterpart to the merabb where camels stay and the land whose grazing is approved.

basis: God feeds his flock and gives it rest
note: The commentary links owner, herd, and the place where animals remain; God promises both to feed his sheep and to make them lie down.

basis: seek the lost and bring back the strayed
note: God’s shepherding promise explicitly seeks the lost and returns the strayed, supplying the caring owner-side of the commentary’s camel left in an unowned place.

basis: Israel is God's pasture flock
note: The commentary links an animal's owner with its herd; Ezekiel closes by identifying Israel as God's human flock and God as their God.

basis: Scattered sheep have no shepherd to seek them
note: The commentary's stray camel remains in a wasteland with no known owner; Ezekiel pictures scattered sheep with no shepherd and no one searching for them.

basis: A mark distinguishes those spared from judgment
note: The commentary's camel brand identifies the animal's owner; Ezekiel's mark distinguishes people to be spared, shifting identification from property to protection.

basis: human rule over living creatures
note: Humanity is told to rule the moving creatures, a creation-account counterpart to the commentary’s Qur’anic picture of livestock made subject to human possession; the biblical verse frames that relation as a commission.

basis: Hebrew ʿābad means to work or serve
note: The commentary labels root ع ب د in naʿbudu and quotes al-baʿīr al-muʿabbad, a tamed/tarred camel; Genesis uses the cognate Hebrew root for the human's work in Eden, preserving a service/work sense without making the garden animal imagery.

basis: speckled and spotted flock as wages
note: Jacob sets visibly marked sheep and goats apart as his wages, so an animal’s visible feature allocates it within a flock to a particular claimant.

basis: Spotted and speckled animals distinguish Jacob's flock
note: The commentary says a brand shows whose camel it is; Jacob proposes coat patterns as a visible way to distinguish which animals are his, though these are natural markings, not brands.

basis: visible color proving ownership or theft
note: Jacob says the flock’s visible coloring will demonstrate his innocence and expose a stolen animal; this makes an animal mark an evidentiary sign of whose it is.

basis: shepherd moderates pace for tender flock
note: Jacob says tender children and nursing flocks cannot be driven hard without losing the herd. It adds a concrete criterion for a leader’s guidance: the front-moving party must accommodate the flock it leads.

basis: trained heifer; fair neck; harness
note: Hosea calls Ephraim a trained heifer and describes placing a yoke on its fair neck for work; this is a close prophetic animal image for the commentary’s muʿabbad camel and its guiding neck.

basis: cords of love; yoke lifted; feeding
note: God leads Israel with cords of kindness and love, lifts the yoke from its jaws, and bends down to feed it. The verse combines animal training, gentle leading, pasture-like provision, and divine compassion.

basis: Stubborn Israel is compared to a heifer and a lamb in pasture
note: The commentary contrasts a tamed camel with straying animals and develops pasture; Hosea calls Israel a stubborn heifer and then invokes a lamb in broad pasture, applying animal behavior to Israel's relation to God.

basis: wild donkey wandering alone
note: Hosea compares political wandering to a wild donkey going alone; it supplies a biblical use of the wild-ass figure for self-directed separation rather than the secure movement of a herd.

basis: Ox knows owner; donkey knows manger
note: The commentary says a stray camel has an unknown owner but livestock recognize their master; Isaiah turns ox and donkey's recognition into a rebuke because Israel does not know its Lord.

basis: ox knows owner; donkey master’s manger
note: Isaiah says an ox knows its owner and a donkey its master’s manger while Israel does not know; it directly parallels the commentary’s claim that livestock recognize owner and place while humans can be more lost.

basis: camel humps carrying treasure through hard country
note: The oracle pictures wealth carried on camels’ humps through a land of distress, a specific Hebrew Bible counterpart to the commentary’s animals carrying burdens to distant places.

basis: Shepherd gathers lambs and gently leads the flock
note: The commentary's lead animal and the request for guidance meet Isaiah's shepherd, who gathers lambs, carries them, and gently leads the nursing ewes.

basis: shepherd feeds, gathers, and gently leads
note: The divine shepherd feeds the flock, gathers lambs, and gently leads nursing ewes; it develops both pasture-care and differentiated leadership within a herd.

basis: unknown paths made straight
note: God leads the blind on an unknown way and makes crooked ground straight, directly pairing guidance with the contrast between a right path and a deviating one.

basis: called by name and declared God’s own
note: The creator calls Israel by name and says “you are mine,” a human counterpart to the commentary’s brand that makes an animal’s belonging and owner recognizable.

basis: compassionate guide leads to water springs
note: The compassionate one leads the hungry and thirsty and guides them by springs of water, a direct guide-and-pasture counterpart to the hādī leading a herd.

basis: All people wander like sheep, each to a separate way
note: The commentary says a camel can stray from its owner and that some people are more astray than animals; Isaiah makes human wandering itself a sheep-going-astray image.

basis: People do not know the way of peace and make crooked paths
note: The commentary pairs the requested straight path with roads that turn aside; Isaiah describes people whose paths are crooked and who therefore do not know peace.

basis: camels bear precious cargo over distance
note: A multitude of camels carries gold and frankincense and brings proclamation of the Lord’s praises; it closely matches the commentary’s load-bearing animals and its hamd/benefit frame.

basis: untrained calf asks to be turned back
note: Ephraim compares itself to an untrained calf and asks God to turn it back. The image gives the commentary’s tamed animal and its loss of direction a penitential human counterpart.

basis: led by water on a straight path without stumbling
note: God promises to lead the returning people by streams of water on a straight way where they will not stumble, binding the commentary’s guidance request, straight path, and animal-water/pasture scene.

basis: Lost sheep are led astray by their shepherds
note: The commentary contrasts a herd's leader with the danger of losing the way; Jeremiah's people are lost sheep whose own shepherds mislead them, making the guide itself culpable.

basis: lost sheep; misleading shepherds; resting place
note: Jeremiah calls the people lost sheep, says their shepherds led them astray, and says they forgot their resting place; it combines the commentary’s stray animal, failed leader, path, and merabb-like place of remaining.

basis: Birds know appointed seasons
note: The commentary contrasts animals that know their owner with people more astray than cattle; Jeremiah says migratory birds know their times while God's people do not know his ordinance.

basis: The wise are put to shame and reject the Lord's word
note: The commentary contrasts animals that recognize an owner with people more astray than cattle; Jeremiah's immediate context extends the bird comparison to the people's rejection of divine instruction.

basis: animals teach the human questioner
note: Job invites the sufferer to ask the animals, which will teach him. This develops the commentary’s secondary reversal in which animal life may disclose what a human who has lost the way fails to know.

basis: The wild ox cannot be harnessed to plow
note: The commentary describes a subdued camel within an owned herd; Job specifies the practical limit of human control over the wild ox.

basis: wild ox bound to furrow and harrow
note: The next question tests whether the wild ox can be bound with a cord to plow and harrow; it supplies the laboring, guided-animal side of the commentary’s mount carried and directed by its body.

basis: The wild donkey is released from its bonds
note: The commentary distinguishes an owned, tamed camel from ownerless wild herds; Job asks who freed the wild donkey, marking its opposite relation to human ownership.

basis: wild ass sent free and unbound
note: Job asks who released the wild ass and loosed its bonds; it gives the commentary’s wild-ass herd a theological counterweight to the tame, owner-marked animal.

basis: The wilderness is the wild donkey's home
note: The commentary's camel is stranded in a desolate place while wild asses live outside owned herds; Job makes the wilderness the wild donkey's dwelling.

basis: wild ass given wilderness as home
note: God gives the wild ass the steppe and salt land as its dwelling, making the wilderness place in the commentary’s lost-animal definition a positive habitat for a creature not domesticated by humans.

basis: The wild donkey searches the mountains for pasture
note: The commentary develops pasture as the place a herd stays and names wild-ass herds; Job gives the untamed animal a mountain range to roam for grazing.

basis: The wild ox will not serve a human master
note: The commentary's dictionary form al-baʿīr al-muʿabbad is a tarred/tamed camel; Job sets against it a wild ox that will not submit to service.

basis: wild ox will not serve or stay at the manger
note: The divine questions ask whether the wild ox will consent to serve a human or spend the night at the manger, directly contrasting a human-owned, tamed herd with a wild bovine beyond ordinary possession.

basis: divine blessing includes six thousand camels
note: The verse calls Job’s latter state blessed and immediately counts his camels among its abundance, closely matching the commentary’s association of camels with niʿma, benefit, and blessing.

basis: divine pity includes much cattle
note: God’s stated pity for Nineveh explicitly includes its many cattle, a concrete biblical companion to the commentary’s move from useful animals to the Lord’s compassion.

basis: Hebrew ʿbd, serving YHWH
note: Hebrew ʿbd is cognate with the commentary’s Arabic ʿ-b-d label; Joshua’s choice to serve the Lord supplies the worship-side use of that family, without transferring the camel-treatment sense into the verse.

basis: A gathered flock crowds its fold
note: The commentary pictures a herd remaining together at its place; Micah portrays the restored remnant gathered like sheep in a fold and pasture.

basis: The king and the Lord go before the gathered people
note: The commentary's malik and hādī are foreleaders followed by the herd; Micah's gate-breaking leader, king, and Lord pass ahead of the flock.

basis: The ark goes ahead to find the people a resting place
note: The commentary's leader walks before a following herd and its pasture is where it stays; Israel's ark travels ahead to seek a place of rest.

basis: what goes ahead seeks a resting place
note: The ark goes before the people to seek out a resting place for them; it binds the front guide to finding the place where the moving community may remain.

basis: Donkey sees the angel and leaves the road
note: The commentary makes guidance a question of following a lead animal; here Balaam's donkey detects the blocked path that the human seer misses, reversing human and animal discernment.

basis: donkey turns aside because it sees the angel
note: Balaam’s donkey leaves the road after seeing the divine messenger while its human rider cannot see and beats it. The scene reverses the surface value of an animal’s turning aside: the animal is the one properly guided, sharpening the commentary’s animal-and-human contrast.

basis: Israel must not be left like sheep without a shepherd
note: The commentary says the request for guidance entails a foreleader whom the rest follow; Moses asks for a successor so the congregation will not be leaderless like sheep.

basis: leader goes out before the people
note: Moses asks for a leader who will go out before and bring the people in, so that they will not be sheep without a shepherd; it applies the commentary’s front-leading herd image to communal guidance.

basis: the righteous know an animal’s needs
note: The righteous person knows the life or needs of his animal, adding responsibility and attention to the commentary’s owner-and-herd relation.

basis: know the condition of flocks and attend to herds
note: The proverb requires careful knowledge of the state of one’s flock and attention to herds, adding the sustained ownerly care absent from the unknown-owner definition of the dālla.

basis: Hebrew noʿam and paths
note: Hebrew noʿam is cognate with the commentary’s n-ʿ-m label, and Wisdom’s ways are called ways of pleasantness; the verse joins the source’s blessing/pleasant-pasture association to a path.

basis: Locusts march in ranks without a king
note: The commentary extends malik to a bee's leader; Proverbs says locusts move together despite having no king, contrasting organized animal following with leaderless coordination.

basis: Ants work without a chief or ruler
note: The commentary names the bee's leader with the source dictionary form melīku; Proverbs supplies a useful contrast in a social insect whose ordered work needs no ruler.

basis: People are God's flock and pasture sheep
note: The commentary connects an animal to its owner; this liturgical line identifies worshippers as God's people and sheep, adding communal belonging to the flock image.

basis: wild asses drink from God’s waters
note: God’s waters give drink to beasts of the field and quench the thirst of wild asses, giving the commentary’s ownerless wild-ass image a providential water-and-habitat setting.

basis: grass grown for cattle
note: God causes grass to grow for cattle, giving the good pasture in the commentary a providential source rather than treating it as only a herd preference.

basis: Wanderers lost in an empty desert without a town
note: The commentary describes a camel escaping and remaining in a desolate place; this psalm opens with people wandering in waste without an inhabited settlement.

basis: The lost cry to the Lord for help
note: The commentary pairs an ownerless animal's lost state with the surah's request for help; here the wilderness wanderers cry out and receive divine rescue.

basis: God leads them by a straight way
note: The commentary makes the camel's foreleader an image for asking to be guided on the straight path; this verse explicitly joins divine leading to a straight way.

basis: A lost sheep asks its owner to seek it
note: The commentary's dālle camel is lost from its owner; the psalmist calls himself a lost sheep and asks God to seek his servant.

basis: lost sheep asks to be sought
note: The speaker says that he has gone astray like a lost sheep and asks the Lord to seek his servant, turning the lost-animal image into a prayer for recovery by the rightful master.

basis: Pleasant boundary lines and a good inheritance
note: The commentary labels root ن ع م and says camels are called en-naʿam for the good and blessing they bring; Hebrew nʿm in this verse describes pleasant boundaries beside a good inheritance, a cognate semantic field rather than an animal term.

basis: Hebrew nʿm means pleasant
note: The commentary labels source root ن ع م and explains en-naʿam through good and blessing; Hebrew nʿm describes pleasantness here, a cognate sense-family rather than a reference to livestock.

basis: The Lord as shepherd; the speaker as sheep
note: The commentary links Rabb to an animal's owner; the psalm names God as shepherd and makes the human speaker part of his flock.

basis: Shepherd settles sheep in green pasture
note: The commentary develops a herd remaining at its pasture and land pleasing for grazing; this verse joins the shepherd's care to settled, nourishing pasture.

basis: YHWH as shepherd
note: The declaration that the Lord is the speaker’s shepherd gives the commentary’s rab/mālik relation its classic pastoral form: a flock has a guiding provider.

basis: God leads on right paths
note: The commentary turns ihdinā into a flock's following its foreleader; the shepherd leads the speaker on right paths, joining guidance to the animal image.

basis: green pastures and resting waters
note: The shepherd makes the sheep lie in green pastures and leads them to resting waters, closely matching the herd’s fixed place and the pasture it finds pleasing.

basis: leading in right tracks
note: The shepherd restores life and leads in right tracks, providing a pastoral analogue to ihdinā and the straight path rather than guidance as a disembodied instruction.

basis: Earth and its fullness belong to the Lord
note: The commentary glosses rabb as the owner of each thing; the psalm states the same universal ownership in a creation hymn.

basis: horse and mule need bit and bridle
note: The psalm contrasts a human who should understand with horse and mule controlled by bridle; its training image usefully complicates the commentary’s tame camel and animal-led guidance without making the two moral claims identical.

basis: God teaches and points out the way
note: The commentary makes ihdinā a request for the leader of a following herd; the psalm has God promise to instruct and guide the person in the way.

basis: Horse and mule need bit and bridle to be guided
note: The commentary treats the flock's voluntarily followed foreleader as an image for guidance; the psalm contrasts an instructed person with animals that must be restrained to come near.

basis: Forest beasts and cattle belong to God
note: The commentary glosses its source form rabb (رَبّ) as owner and begins with an owned camel herd; this verse explicitly places wild beasts and cattle under divine ownership.

basis: all cattle belong to God
note: God declares every forest beast and the cattle on a thousand hills to be his, a direct biblical counterpart to the commentary’s claim that every creature has its rab/mālik.

basis: The world and all in it belong to God
note: The commentary's source gloss says the Rabb of each thing is its owner; the psalm applies ownership universally, beyond a single herd.

basis: God leads his people like a flock through the wilderness
note: The commentary's flock follows its leading animal; the psalm depicts God leading his people as sheep through a wilderness journey.

basis: people led like sheep through wilderness
note: God leads the people out like sheep and guides them like a flock in the wilderness, directly joining flock, guidance, and a journey through exposed country.

basis: David is taken from ewes to shepherd Israel
note: The commentary's malik is the animal ahead of a herd; this verse makes a former shepherd the ruler appointed over God's people.

basis: David shepherds and guides with integrity
note: The commentary joins a lead animal to guidance of those following; this verse presents Israel's ruler as one who shepherds and guides the people.

basis: Sheep, oxen, and wild beasts are under human rule
note: The commentary distinguishes owned livestock from wild herds; the psalm specifies domestic flock and oxen alongside beasts of the field under human dominion.

basis: People are God's pasture flock and hear his voice
note: The commentary joins herd ownership to following a leader; the psalm calls the people sheep of God's hand and immediately calls them to hear his voice.

basis: where the shepherd pastures and lets flock rest
note: The beloved asks where the shepherd pastures his flock and makes it lie down at noon, directly matching the commentary’s owner, grazing place, and place of remaining.

basis: follow flock tracks and pasture kids near shepherd tents
note: The reply directs the seeker to go out by the tracks of the flock and pasture her kids beside shepherds’ tents; it gives an unusually exact literary image of following a herd’s route toward a shepherded grazing place.

basis: People wander like sheep because there is no shepherd
note: The commentary makes the request for guidance a need for a foreleader; Zechariah explains the people's wandering by the absence of a shepherd.

basis: flock wanders for lack of shepherd
note: The people wander like sheep and suffer because there is no shepherd, making the absence of the commentary’s front-leading, responsible figure the stated cause of dispersion.

basis: When the shepherd is struck, the sheep scatter
note: The commentary says a herd follows its foreleader; Zechariah gives the contrary scene in which losing that leader disperses the flock.

basis: Wisdom guides on straight paths
note: Wisdom guides the righteous person on straight paths in its account of divine guidance; it supplies a Jewish Second Temple formulation for the commentary’s moving sense of the straight path.

basis: All things are God's own
note: The commentary's source gloss calls the Rabb of everything its owner; Wisdom grounds God's sparing care in the claim that all things belong to him.
